newsitem.title: PERU: Peru set to bury its dead as Japan thanks Fujimori.
newsitem.headline: Peru set to bury its dead as Japan thanks Fujimori.

text.p: Peru prepared to bury its dead on Thursday as Japan's Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda arrived in Lima with congratulations for President Alberto Fujimori on the assault that ended the four-month hostage crisis.

State funerals were scheduled during the morning for judge Carlos Giusti, who bled to death after being caught by a bullet, and two other troops killed during the storming of the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence.

The bodies of the 14 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels, slain by bombs and gunfire in a 40-minute battle, were taken to a Lima morgue where their families would be allowed to collect them.
Although praise flooded in from around the world for the crack troops who rescued the 71 VIP hostages, pressure grew on Fujimori's government to reveal exactly how Giusti died.

There was speculation he may have been accidentally struck by a military bullet during an otherwise clinically executed operation that was compared with Israel's legendary 1976 raid to free hijack victims in Entebbe, Uganda.

The president of the Lima chamber of lawyers, Vladimir Paz de la Barra, called for an investigation, saying it was strange a tourniquet was not applied to Giusti's bleeding leg. "I think these cases should be clarified," Paz de la Barra said.
Japan, whose two dozen nationals were all unharmed in the operation, was fulsome in its praise despite not being consulted before the raid on what was legally its territory.

Ikeda flew in to pass on Tokyo's thanks to Fujimori and hear firsthand about the daring assault. His 100-strong delegation included 27 police officers, six members of a medical team and 10 relatives of freed Japanese captives.
After meeting Fujimori and attending the funerals, Ikeda was slated later to meet Japanese Ambassador Morihisa Aoki, host of the ill-fated Dec. 17 cocktail party stormed by the MRTA.

In brief comments to reporters, Ikeda said he would discuss with Peruvian authorities how to avoid a repeat of the hostage crisis, which saw a group of Marxist rebels hold Peruvian, Bolivian and Japanese VIPs for 126 days to demand the release of jailed comrades.

In Tokyo, Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto said he also planned to visit Peru shortly to reiterate his gratitude. "I would like to thank Peru from the bottom of my heart for thoroughly preparing for the raid and successfully freeing most of the hostages," Hashimoto told the Lower House of parliament.
Tokyo had consistently urged Fujimori to seek a peaceful end to the standoff, and had sent Ikeda to Peru in the early days of the crisis to ensure restraint.
But Fujimori's patience finally wore out when the MRTA decided to limit medical visits to the captives.

As commandos swarmed into the building from all sides and at least five tunnels where they had been waiting for several days, MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini shouted: "We've screwed up! We've screwed up!," the daily La Republica reported on Thursday.

The two teenage girls among the guerrilla band shouted at troops to hold fire saying "We Surrender! We Surrender!", the paper added, citing police sources who had been listening in with electronic surveillance at the time of the attack.
But the order was shoot to kill.
The successful operation reversed overnight Fujimori's popularity rating, according to polling agency Apoyo SA.
A survey conducted the day after the raid showed his approval level shot up to 67 percent from 38 percent four days ago, the lowest level during his seven years in office.
The poll of 420 people in metropolitan Lima, where about one-third of Peruvians live, showed 84 percent approved of the assault on the residence.
But even some of Fujimori's supporters expected the euphoria and worldwide praise for the raid to fade soon, saying he still faced a litany of problems in this poor, crisis-ridden country.

"Every government has its ups and downs. I wouldn't expect this rise in its popularity to last long, certainly not two or three years," said congressman Carlos Ferrero of Fujimori's Cambio '90-New Majority party.
The raid gave Peru's military one of the biggest victories ever in its fratricidal, 17-year war with leftist rebels, in which about 30,000 people have died.
Cleanup operations continued at the gutted residence, where police were sweeping the grounds for landmines and booby traps.

With the bloodied corpses of the Marxist rebels still lying where they died, Fujimori toured the gutted mansion on Wednesday. Peruvian television showed grisly images of him inspecting the house and stepping gingerly past the body of guerrilla leader Cerpa Cartolini -- a bullet hole in his head and a gash across his neck.
The few hostages willing to talk publicly during their first full day of freedom spoke of a depressing life under MRTA guns, coping with rats, cold food and bullying rebels.

One hostage said the rebels continually ran the 72 captives through drills in case of assault. The drills would end with the guerrillas pointing their weapons at captives bunched into small groups and threatening to blow them up.

"They made us believe they were all carrying explosives," said the liberated hostage, congressman Carlos Blanco, adding that Cerpa "always had an aggressive attitude and the most profound disdain for human life."
